title: What If You Fell Into a Black Hole? | What If #4
thought_experiment: Labelled thought experiment: a person falls straight into a non-spinning black hole of ten solar masses from 5,000 km above the event horizon. Simplified Newtonian tidal model; no radiation, accretion disk or spin.

hook_candidates.text: Jump into this black hole. Will you arrive in one piece?
You're falling into a black hole. Your feet are falling faster.
A black hole stretches you like spaghetti before you reach it.
Small black holes are deadlier than giant ones. Why?
Watch this counter. It hits zero at the edge of a black hole.

parts.text: Will you arrive in one piece?
The edge is five thousand kilometers down.
so they're pulled harder than your head.
You stretch long and squeeze thin,
A bigger black hole is gentler.
and you cross the edge in one piece,
but you can never get out.

sources: Mechanism: the part of a body nearer the black hole feels a stronger pull than the part farther away; the body is stretched lengthwise and compressed sideways (spaghettification). NASA Science, 'What Happens When Something Gets Too Close to a Black Hole?', https://science.nasa.gov/universe/black-holes/what-happens-when-something-gets-too-close-to-a-black-hole/ ; Wikipedia 'Spaghettification' (gravity at feet stronger than head, vertically stretched, horizontally compressed).

Stellar black holes spaghettify an astronaut before the event horizon; at a supermassive one an astronaut may cross the horizon without noticing, but once inside falling to the centre is inevitable: Wikipedia 'Spaghettification', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaghettification

Small black holes have far stronger tides at the horizon than big ones; 1 solar mass: horizon radius 2.9 km, tide on a 1.8 m person about 19.6 billion m/s^2; 100 million solar masses: horizon radius 295 million km, tide about 0.0000019 m/s^2. Astronomy magazine, Ask Astro, Feb 2023, https://www.astronomy.com/science/ask-astro-why-are-small-black-holes-more-dangerous-than-big-ones/

Ten solar masses (labelled choice, a typical stellar-mass black hole): horizon radius = 2GM/c^2 = 29.5 km. Start point 5,000 km above the horizon (labelled choice). Tidal stretch on a 1.8 m person, a = 2GML/r^3: about 4 g at the start, about 450 g at 1,000 km, about 19 million g at the horizon (consistent with Astronomy's 1-solar-mass figure scaled by 1/M^2). Arithmetic.
Simplified: Newtonian tidal formula, non-spinning hole; the 'giant' shown is 100 million solar masses as in the Astronomy example.
comment_question: Would you rather fall into a small black hole or a giant one?
